de.content:
The consumer data broker Radaris.com has long had a reputation for ignoring requests to remove personal information from its vast empire of people-search services online. That reputation caught up with the company recently in a lawsuit alleging Radaris violated a New Jersey privacy law that provides for hefty fines against data brokers that publish personal information on state law enforcement officials. In the face of repeated stonewalling and prevarication by attorneys for Radaris, the judge in the case ordered that radaris.com and more than a dozen other data broker domains be transferred to the plaintiffs.

The radaris.com website, prior to the domain transfer to Atlas.

In February 2024, Radaris was sued by Atlas Data Privacy Corp, a company that has been pursuing data brokers alleged to be violating a New Jersey statute called Daniel’s Law. The statute allows state law enforcement officials, government personnel, judges and their families to have their information completely removed from commercial data brokers and people-search services, and provides for fines of $1,000 per violation against companies that ignore removal requests.

Less than a month after Atlas sued Radaris, KrebsOnSecurity published a deep dive into the Radaris co-founders — Igor and Dmitry Lubarsky (also spelled Lybarsky) — Russian-born brothers living in Massachusetts who operate a dizzying array of people-search companies as well as a number of Russian language dating services and affiliate programs.

Attorneys for the Lubarsky brothers threatened to sue for defamation if the story wasn’t removed and an apology issued. Their attorney asserted that our reporting was wildly inaccurate, and that the true owners of the company were Ukrainians living in Ukraine.

The Lubarsky brothers Dmitry or “Dan” (left) and Gary/Igor.

KrebsOnSecurity doubled down and showed how the Lubarsky brothers built and operated Radaris and other data broker companies using a fictitious CEO’s name. Our follow-up story noted that Radaris’s attorney — a lawyer with the Boston Law Group named Val Gurvits — admitted his clients had invented the CEO pseudonym “Gary Norden,” and that Radaris also had issued multiple press releases over the years that quoted the fake CEO while seeking money from potential investors.

Attorneys for Radaris waited until the last minute to appear in court and contest what was all but certain to be a default judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, and then told the court that Atlas had failed to serve the real owners and operators of Radaris and several of its sister data broker companies.

Atlas re-filed the lawsuit in June 2025, this time dramatically expanding the number of Radaris family data brokers accused of violating Daniel’s Law. Matt Adkisson, president and CEO of Atlas, said Radaris turned to a tried-and-true playbook: Delaying in court until the last possible minute, and playing shell games with Radaris’s true country of origin and the individuals listed as owners and operators of these sites.

“We refer to this period as their island-hopping phase. Privacy policies changed constantly, and new entities kept appearing from places like the Marshall Islands, the British Virgin Islands, and Seychelles,” Adkisson told KrebsOnSecurity. “Behind the scenes, it felt like a shell game. Defense lawyers told the court that certain entities merely operated the domains and were the proper parties to sue. But by the time a judgment neared, those entities would be discarded and new entities would appear. Meanwhile, the lawyers claimed the other entities that actually owned the domains should not be held responsible.”

Adkisson said when the defendants updated their terms of service to state that Radaris was suddenly managed by a company in the Marshall Islands, Atlas hired an investigator in that country and soon learned the brand new entity that Radaris claimed was managing the company didn’t even exist yet.

Mr. Gurvits stepped forward as Radaris’s attorney in a class action lawsuit the company temporarily lost in 2017 because it never contested the claim in court. When the plaintiffs told the judge they couldn’t collect on the $7.5 million default judgment, the court ordered the domain registry Verisign to transfer the radaris.com domain name to the plaintiffs.

Mr. Gurvits appealed that verdict, arguing the lawsuit hadn’t named the actual owners of the Radaris domain name — a Cyprus company called Bitseller Expert Limited — and thus taking the domain away would be a violation of their due process rights.

The judge in the 2017 case ruled in Radaris’ favor — halting the domain transfer — and told the plaintiffs they could refile their complaint. Soon after, the operator of Radaris changed from Bitseller to Andtop Company, an entity formed (PDF) in the Marshall Islands in Oct. 2020. The plaintiffs never re-filed their lawsuit.

A mind map of various entities tied to Radaris and the company’s co-founders. Click to enlarge.

“That seemed to be their modus operandi,” said Raj Parikh, a partner at PEM Law in New Jersey who handles most of the Daniel’s Law litigation for Atlas. “In the past, they won by attrition. Plaintiffs’ attorneys tired of the procedural games and just gave up. That strategy worked for a decade, and it probably would have worked in this case too, since any financial recovery from foreign actors will be difficult. But we were acutely aware of the threat this website posed to law enforcement officers and other public officials in New Jersey, and decided early on to commit whatever time and resources were necessary to remove that threat.”

On August 26, the judge in the New Jersey case found the defendants were given multiple chances to appear and defend the claims against them but had failed to do so. Mr. Gurvits declined to comment on the case, saying it had been assigned to another attorney, a Mr. Victor Worms. In response to questions, Mr. Worms asserted the New Jersey court transferred Radaris.com to Atlas as part of a default judgment against Radaris.com, which is not a legal entity.

“We have made a motion to vacate that default judgment on the grounds that it is void since a non-entity has no legal capacity to sue or be sued,” Worms replied. “We also intend to pursue all appropriate appeals because we believe the transfer of Radaris.com amounts to a forfeiture in violation of various constitutional principles.”

While radaris.com still comes up prominently in results when searching online for U.S. residents by name, the domain no longer sells detailed personal dossiers on millions of Americans. Its homepage now displays a notice from Atlas, as well as links to our previous reporting on Radaris.

Atlas told KrebsOnSecurity that it has obtained more than 10,000 emails and documents in the course of litigation, and that those messages confirm our previous reporting on the owners and operators of Radaris and its myriad companies.

Atlas said the emails clearly establish that the nominal legal vehicles — Radaris America, Inc.; Bitseller Expert Limited; Digital Orbit Corp; Core Solutions Group Inc; Lucky Solutions Inc; Virtura Corp; Veripages Inc.; Nuform Solutions Inc.; Growth Data Advisors Inc.; Property Experts, Inc — are all administered by the same three or four people from the same mailboxes, share one bank or payment card set, and are all managed from one virtual office address.

“The corpus establishes, with documentary evidence generated independently by banks, payment processors, hosting providers, registrars, software-as-a-service vendors and the operators’ own systems, that radaris.com and at least twenty-five other people-search websites are one operation run by a small Boston-area group whose administrative, financial and technical functions sit on the difive.com mail domain and its successors (centerex.com, scienteco.com, eprofit.com, realmo.com, pub360.com),” reads a summary shared by Atlas.

Atlas said the emails show Radaris.com earns approximately $42,000 a month, while Veripages.com earns around $45,000 monthly via its partnership with the Lifetime Value Company, a marketing and advertising firm whose brands include PeopleLooker, PeopleSmart, NumberGuru, and Bumper, a car history site.

According to Atlas, the emails also showed the Radaris family of websites earns as much as $25,000 each month from their partnership with Onerep, a company that claims to help people remove their information from people-search sites. In March 2024, KrebsOnSecurity revealed how the Belarusian founder of Onerep had launched and operated dozens of people-search sites over the years and was continuing to operate one of them (Nuwber), effectively spreading the disease and selling the cure.

The domain radaris.com now redirects to this notice from Atlas about the court-ordered domain transfer.

All told, the New Jersey court has so far transferred 14 domain names from the Radaris family of companies to Atlas. Radaris.com now redirects to a notice of the court-ordered domain transfer.

The Radaris family of companies is still potentially facing fines of $1,000 per alleged violation of Daniel’s Law. For the time being, however, Daniel’s Law is facing a constitutional challenge from virtually all of the 150 other consumer data broker firms being sued by Atlas.

The data broker industry responded by having at least 70 of the Atlas lawsuits moved to federal court, challenging the New Jersey statute as overly broad and a violation of the First Amendment. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has not yet issued a decision on the constitutional challenge, but either way the case is widely expected to be appealed all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, at least 14 other states have now passed laws modeled after the New Jersey statute, with more states considering similar measures. However, West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law was ruled facially unconstitutional under the First Amendment by a federal district court in August 2025.

Justin Sherman is a privacy expert and author of the forthcoming book “The Middlemen,” which examines how the data broker industry powers modern surveillance. Sherman said federal lawmakers have long faced intense lobbying by the technology industry against more restrictive U.S. data privacy laws, but that many powerful industries are now working against passing comprehensive data privacy legislation.

“These days at the federal level, add in the intense amount of lobbying against these laws from social media companies, big tech, cryptocurrency firms, and now AI proponents in the mix who claim that limiting their data scraping is somehow going to collapse the whole U.S. economy under Chinese rule,” he said.

Sherman said people-search companies will continue to thrive unless and until Congress enacts meaningful consumer privacy and data protection laws that are relevant to life in the 21st century. That’s because virtually all state privacy laws exempt records that might be considered “public” or “government” documents, including voting registries, property filings, marriage certificates, motor vehicle records, criminal records, court documents, death records, professional licenses, bankruptcy filings, and more.

We’ve had eight million wake-up calls already on the need for better privacy laws. The lack of comprehensive federal privacy law is not for a lack of knowledge, and anyone claiming otherwise is either not reading the news or kidding themselves.”

ru.title: Data Broker Radaris Loses Domains in Privacy Fight
ru.summary: The consumer data broker Radaris.com has long had a reputation for ignoring requests to remove personal information from its vast empire of people-search services online. That reputation caught up with the company recently in a lawsuit alleging Radar
ru.content:
The consumer data broker Radaris.com has long had a reputation for ignoring requests to remove personal information from its vast empire of people-search services online. That reputation caught up with the company recently in a lawsuit alleging Radaris violated a New Jersey privacy law that provides for hefty fines against data brokers that publish personal information on state law enforcement officials. In the face of repeated stonewalling and prevarication by attorneys for Radaris, the judge in the case ordered that radaris.com and more than a dozen other data broker domains be transferred to the plaintiffs.

The radaris.com website, prior to the domain transfer to Atlas.

In February 2024, Radaris was sued by Atlas Data Privacy Corp, a company that has been pursuing data brokers alleged to be violating a New Jersey statute called Daniel’s Law. The statute allows state law enforcement officials, government personnel, judges and their families to have their information completely removed from commercial data brokers and people-search services, and provides for fines of $1,000 per violation against companies that ignore removal requests.

Less than a month after Atlas sued Radaris, KrebsOnSecurity published a deep dive into the Radaris co-founders — Igor and Dmitry Lubarsky (also spelled Lybarsky) — Russian-born brothers living in Massachusetts who operate a dizzying array of people-search companies as well as a number of Russian language dating services and affiliate programs.

Attorneys for the Lubarsky brothers threatened to sue for defamation if the story wasn’t removed and an apology issued. Their attorney asserted that our reporting was wildly inaccurate, and that the true owners of the company were Ukrainians living in Ukraine.

The Lubarsky brothers Dmitry or “Dan” (left) and Gary/Igor.

KrebsOnSecurity doubled down and showed how the Lubarsky brothers built and operated Radaris and other data broker companies using a fictitious CEO’s name. Our follow-up story noted that Radaris’s attorney — a lawyer with the Boston Law Group named Val Gurvits — admitted his clients had invented the CEO pseudonym “Gary Norden,” and that Radaris also had issued multiple press releases over the years that quoted the fake CEO while seeking money from potential investors.

Attorneys for Radaris waited until the last minute to appear in court and contest what was all but certain to be a default judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, and then told the court that Atlas had failed to serve the real owners and operators of Radaris and several of its sister data broker companies.

Atlas re-filed the lawsuit in June 2025, this time dramatically expanding the number of Radaris family data brokers accused of violating Daniel’s Law. Matt Adkisson, president and CEO of Atlas, said Radaris turned to a tried-and-true playbook: Delaying in court until the last possible minute, and playing shell games with Radaris’s true country of origin and the individuals listed as owners and operators of these sites.

“We refer to this period as their island-hopping phase. Privacy policies changed constantly, and new entities kept appearing from places like the Marshall Islands, the British Virgin Islands, and Seychelles,” Adkisson told KrebsOnSecurity. “Behind the scenes, it felt like a shell game. Defense lawyers told the court that certain entities merely operated the domains and were the proper parties to sue. But by the time a judgment neared, those entities would be discarded and new entities would appear. Meanwhile, the lawyers claimed the other entities that actually owned the domains should not be held responsible.”

Adkisson said when the defendants updated their terms of service to state that Radaris was suddenly managed by a company in the Marshall Islands, Atlas hired an investigator in that country and soon learned the brand new entity that Radaris claimed was managing the company didn’t even exist yet.

Mr. Gurvits stepped forward as Radaris’s attorney in a class action lawsuit the company temporarily lost in 2017 because it never contested the claim in court. When the plaintiffs told the judge they couldn’t collect on the $7.5 million default judgment, the court ordered the domain registry Verisign to transfer the radaris.com domain name to the plaintiffs.

Mr. Gurvits appealed that verdict, arguing the lawsuit hadn’t named the actual owners of the Radaris domain name — a Cyprus company called Bitseller Expert Limited — and thus taking the domain away would be a violation of their due process rights.

The judge in the 2017 case ruled in Radaris’ favor — halting the domain transfer — and told the plaintiffs they could refile their complaint. Soon after, the operator of Radaris changed from Bitseller to Andtop Company, an entity formed (PDF) in the Marshall Islands in Oct. 2020. The plaintiffs never re-filed their lawsuit.

A mind map of various entities tied to Radaris and the company’s co-founders. Click to enlarge.

“That seemed to be their modus operandi,” said Raj Parikh, a partner at PEM Law in New Jersey who handles most of the Daniel’s Law litigation for Atlas. “In the past, they won by attrition. Plaintiffs’ attorneys tired of the procedural games and just gave up. That strategy worked for a decade, and it probably would have worked in this case too, since any financial recovery from foreign actors will be difficult. But we were acutely aware of the threat this website posed to law enforcement officers and other public officials in New Jersey, and decided early on to commit whatever time and resources were necessary to remove that threat.”

On August 26, the judge in the New Jersey case found the defendants were given multiple chances to appear and defend the claims against them but had failed to do so. Mr. Gurvits declined to comment on the case, saying it had been assigned to another attorney, a Mr. Victor Worms. In response to questions, Mr. Worms asserted the New Jersey court transferred Radaris.com to Atlas as part of a default judgment against Radaris.com, which is not a legal entity.

“We have made a motion to vacate that default judgment on the grounds that it is void since a non-entity has no legal capacity to sue or be sued,” Worms replied. “We also intend to pursue all appropriate appeals because we believe the transfer of Radaris.com amounts to a forfeiture in violation of various constitutional principles.”

While radaris.com still comes up prominently in results when searching online for U.S. residents by name, the domain no longer sells detailed personal dossiers on millions of Americans. Its homepage now displays a notice from Atlas, as well as links to our previous reporting on Radaris.

Atlas told KrebsOnSecurity that it has obtained more than 10,000 emails and documents in the course of litigation, and that those messages confirm our previous reporting on the owners and operators of Radaris and its myriad companies.

Atlas said the emails clearly establish that the nominal legal vehicles — Radaris America, Inc.; Bitseller Expert Limited; Digital Orbit Corp; Core Solutions Group Inc; Lucky Solutions Inc; Virtura Corp; Veripages Inc.; Nuform Solutions Inc.; Growth Data Advisors Inc.; Property Experts, Inc — are all administered by the same three or four people from the same mailboxes, share one bank or payment card set, and are all managed from one virtual office address.

“The corpus establishes, with documentary evidence generated independently by banks, payment processors, hosting providers, registrars, software-as-a-service vendors and the operators’ own systems, that radaris.com and at least twenty-five other people-search websites are one operation run by a small Boston-area group whose administrative, financial and technical functions sit on the difive.com mail domain and its successors (centerex.com, scienteco.com, eprofit.com, realmo.com, pub360.com),” reads a summary shared by Atlas.

Atlas said the emails show Radaris.com earns approximately $42,000 a month, while Veripages.com earns around $45,000 monthly via its partnership with the Lifetime Value Company, a marketing and advertising firm whose brands include PeopleLooker, PeopleSmart, NumberGuru, and Bumper, a car history site.

According to Atlas, the emails also showed the Radaris family of websites earns as much as $25,000 each month from their partnership with Onerep, a company that claims to help people remove their information from people-search sites. In March 2024, KrebsOnSecurity revealed how the Belarusian founder of Onerep had launched and operated dozens of people-search sites over the years and was continuing to operate one of them (Nuwber), effectively spreading the disease and selling the cure.

The domain radaris.com now redirects to this notice from Atlas about the court-ordered domain transfer.

All told, the New Jersey court has so far transferred 14 domain names from the Radaris family of companies to Atlas. Radaris.com now redirects to a notice of the court-ordered domain transfer.

The Radaris family of companies is still potentially facing fines of $1,000 per alleged violation of Daniel’s Law. For the time being, however, Daniel’s Law is facing a constitutional challenge from virtually all of the 150 other consumer data broker firms being sued by Atlas.

The data broker industry responded by having at least 70 of the Atlas lawsuits moved to federal court, challenging the New Jersey statute as overly broad and a violation of the First Amendment. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has not yet issued a decision on the constitutional challenge, but either way the case is widely expected to be appealed all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, at least 14 other states have now passed laws modeled after the New Jersey statute, with more states considering similar measures. However, West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law was ruled facially unconstitutional under the First Amendment by a federal district court in August 2025.

Justin Sherman is a privacy expert and author of the forthcoming book “The Middlemen,” which examines how the data broker industry powers modern surveillance. Sherman said federal lawmakers have long faced intense lobbying by the technology industry against more restrictive U.S. data privacy laws, but that many powerful industries are now working against passing comprehensive data privacy legislation.

“These days at the federal level, add in the intense amount of lobbying against these laws from social media companies, big tech, cryptocurrency firms, and now AI proponents in the mix who claim that limiting their data scraping is somehow going to collapse the whole U.S. economy under Chinese rule,” he said.

Sherman said people-search companies will continue to thrive unless and until Congress enacts meaningful consumer privacy and data protection laws that are relevant to life in the 21st century. That’s because virtually all state privacy laws exempt records that might be considered “public” or “government” documents, including voting registries, property filings, marriage certificates, motor vehicle records, criminal records, court documents, death records, professional licenses, bankruptcy filings, and more.

At least 25 states have passed or implemented laws requiring age verification for residents seeking to access adult content online, but there is no federal law that limits how the companies that are scanning everyone’s drivers license can use, share or keep the data provided. Had such restrictions been enshrined in law, we may have avoided the recent breach at IDScan.net, which exposed the drivers license information on more than 153 million Americans when the records were briefly turned into a point-and-click identity theft service on the dark web.

“The average person can look at Daniel’s Law and have a perfectly normal reaction, which is that everyone should be covered, not just police and judges,” Sherman said. “But we don’t need more wake-up calls. We’ve had eight million wake-up calls already on the need for better privacy laws. The lack of comprehensive federal privacy law is not for a lack of knowledge, and anyone claiming otherwise is either not reading the news or kidding themselves.”

articles.title: Hackers Hijack OVHcloud GitHub Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware
articles.summary: Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases.
articles.content:
Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases.

The October 19, 2026, supply chain attack targeted users downloading the OVHcloud CLI, with malware designed to collect secrets stored on their computers. A customer spotted suspicious release changes and alerted the cloud provider, which blocked the malicious files within 94 minutes.

OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba said the affected releases were v0.11.0, v0.12.0, v0.13.0, v0.14.0, and v0.15.0. He identified v0.10.0 as clean and announced a safe v0.16.0 release. That replacement is now available on the project’s official GitHub releases page, where it is marked as immutable, meaning its published release files cannot be changed.

## OVHcloud Supply Chain Attack

According to Klaba’s account, the compromised files appeared at 14:47 and were detected and blocked at 16:21. OVHcloud’s initial checks found no other affected repository. Those findings limit the confirmed scope to the CLI project, rather than establishing a wider breach across the company’s GitHub organization or cloud platform.

The attacker used an existing developer account to add a malicious binary to the software distributed through GitHub. This placed the threat inside a trusted download location, giving users little reason to suspect that a routine CLI download could expose local credentials. OVHcloud has not explained how the developer account was first compromised.

The customer’s report raised concerns about release files being replaced with a “dirty build” of a later commit. In software builds, that label generally signals changes beyond the recorded source revision. The public issue listing identifies the report as issue #300, covering replaced assets for v0.13.0 through v0.15.0. OVHcloud’s warning named two additional affected versions.

The customer also questioned the account behind the changes and asked whether release files should be locked against replacement. They said they had switched to building through the Go module proxy while seeking clarification. Their report was public because the repository lacked a private vulnerability reporting channel.

Klaba described the added program as a binary whose job was to retrieve secrets from disk. He said its quality was poor but warned that it could still achieve its purpose. The available disclosure does not establish which files it searched, where collected data was sent, or how many users executed the malicious downloads.

The CLI’s normal role makes this threat especially serious. OVHcloud documents the tool as a way to manage cloud services, account resources, and automated workflows. Its supported authentication methods include a local .ovh.conf file containing credentials, alongside environment variables for application keys, application secrets, and consumer keys.

Those documented credential locations explain why a compromised administration tool can create risks beyond the downloaded program itself. However, they are not a confirmed list of this malware’s targets. Until OVHcloud publishes its technical findings, specific claims about stolen SSH keys, browser passwords, persistence, or attacker infrastructure would go beyond the evidence.

The incident fits the broader pattern covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s reporting on trusted software updates used to steal developer and cloud credentials. Attackers can use stolen publishing access to turn familiar software delivery channels into routes for credential theft, without needing users to visit a fake website.

OVHcloud urged users who downloaded the CLI during the incident to update it immediately or delete it. Klaba also advised affected users to change all secrets stored on disk. Rotation is important because replacing the malicious program does not cancel credentials that may already have been copied.

Organizations investigating possible exposure should identify which machines downloaded and ran affected files, preserve available evidence, and review account activity tied to potentially exposed credentials. Their response should extend beyond OVHcloud credentials if other secrets were accessible on those machines. The company’s warning covers local secrets broadly, not only its own service keys.

A related GhostAction GitHub credential theft campaign shows why repository access deserves close attention. That campaign used stolen accounts to introduce malicious workflows under trusted identities. No evidence currently links it to the OVHcloud incident. For OVHcloud users, the immediate priorities remain replacing affected downloads and renewing potentially exposed secrets while the company continues its malware investigation and publishes further technical findings.

tr.summary: Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases.
tr.content:
Hackers compromised the GitHub account of an OVHcloud developer and used it to distribute malicious files through the company’s official command-line tool releases.

The October 19, 2026, supply chain attack targeted users downloading the OVHcloud CLI, with malware designed to collect secrets stored on their computers. A customer spotted suspicious release changes and alerted the cloud provider, which blocked the malicious files within 94 minutes.

OVHcloud CEO Octave Klaba said the affected releases were v0.11.0, v0.12.0, v0.13.0, v0.14.0, and v0.15.0. He identified v0.10.0 as clean and announced a safe v0.16.0 release. That replacement is now available on the project’s official GitHub releases page, where it is marked as immutable, meaning its published release files cannot be changed.

## OVHcloud Supply Chain Attack

According to Klaba’s account, the compromised files appeared at 14:47 and were detected and blocked at 16:21. OVHcloud’s initial checks found no other affected repository. Those findings limit the confirmed scope to the CLI project, rather than establishing a wider breach across the company’s GitHub organization or cloud platform.

The attacker used an existing developer account to add a malicious binary to the software distributed through GitHub. This placed the threat inside a trusted download location, giving users little reason to suspect that a routine CLI download could expose local credentials. OVHcloud has not explained how the developer account was first compromised.

The customer’s report raised concerns about release files being replaced with a “dirty build” of a later commit. In software builds, that label generally signals changes beyond the recorded source revision. The public issue listing identifies the report as issue #300, covering replaced assets for v0.13.0 through v0.15.0. OVHcloud’s warning named two additional affected versions.

The customer also questioned the account behind the changes and asked whether release files should be locked against replacement. They said they had switched to building through the Go module proxy while seeking clarification. Their report was public because the repository lacked a private vulnerability reporting channel.

Klaba described the added program as a binary whose job was to retrieve secrets from disk. He said its quality was poor but warned that it could still achieve its purpose. The available disclosure does not establish which files it searched, where collected data was sent, or how many users executed the malicious downloads.

The CLI’s normal role makes this threat especially serious. OVHcloud documents the tool as a way to manage cloud services, account resources, and automated workflows. Its supported authentication methods include a local .ovh.conf file containing credentials, alongside environment variables for application keys, application secrets, and consumer keys.

Those documented credential locations explain why a compromised administration tool can create risks beyond the downloaded program itself. However, they are not a confirmed list of this malware’s targets. Until OVHcloud publishes its technical findings, specific claims about stolen SSH keys, browser passwords, persistence, or attacker infrastructure would go beyond the evidence.

The incident fits the broader pattern covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s reporting on trusted software updates used to steal developer and cloud credentials. Attackers can use stolen publishing access to turn familiar software delivery channels into routes for credential theft, without needing users to visit a fake website.

OVHcloud urged users who downloaded the CLI during the incident to update it immediately or delete it. Klaba also advised affected users to change all secrets stored on disk. Rotation is important because replacing the malicious program does not cancel credentials that may already have been copied.

Organizations investigating possible exposure should identify which machines downloaded and ran affected files, preserve available evidence, and review account activity tied to potentially exposed credentials. Their response should extend beyond OVHcloud credentials if other secrets were accessible on those machines. The company’s warning covers local secrets broadly, not only its own service keys.

A related GhostAction GitHub credential theft campaign shows why repository access deserves close attention. That campaign used stolen accounts to introduce malicious workflows under trusted identities. No evidence currently links it to the OVHcloud incident. For OVHcloud users, the immediate priorities remain replacing affected downloads and renewing potentially exposed secrets while the company continues its malware investigation and publishes further technical findings.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates for Just 5 Minutes to Secretly Install Backdoors
articles.summary: A short-lived change to AOMEI’s software update system gave hackers a way to deliver malware through a trusted route.
articles.content:
A short-lived change to AOMEI’s software update system gave hackers a way to deliver malware through a trusted route.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant found that attackers repeatedly altered AOMEI’s update settings for only a few minutes at a time between April and July 2026.

Any AOMEI Backupper computer checking for updates during an active window could receive a malicious download instead of a genuine update.

The operation did not rely on a software flaw or require users to open a suspicious file. Instead, the attackers changed two configuration files on AOMEI’s servers, redirecting downloads and using the program’s notification feature to run the malware.

Affected organizations were reported across several sectors and countries, including India, though the full number of impacted systems is not known.

Google Cloud’s GTIG and Mandiant analysts tracked the malware chain as CROSSROAD and SHINYROAD and attributed the activity to a threat group they call UNC7017.

The initial activity was first detected through telemetry shared by ManageEngine’s Threat Analysis Lab, which observed suspicious behavior in late May. AOMEI told Google that it had taken corrective action to secure its distribution servers.

## Hackers Hijack AOMEI Software Updates

AOMEI’s update process uses down_html.ini to provide a package version, checksum and download location. A separate file, Notifycfg.ini, guides its notification service, including which local programs to run.

During observed tampering periods, attackers changed both files so the software would accept and launch a harmful ZIP archive.

Researchers recorded three specific windows: ten minutes on May 28, six minutes on July 16 and five minutes on July 20. The attackers restored the original settings after each window.

That made ordinary checks of the live update server less useful: an investigation carried out later could see only the clean files.

The method differs from incidents involving altered software releases or build systems; a Notepad++ update breach is another example of attackers targeting the route that delivers trusted software.

The brief windows did not make the malware itself temporary. A computer that received the altered instructions could continue running malicious files after AOMEI’s servers were repaired.

In July, the attackers also directed one download through a public Google Cloud Storage bucket, after earlier use of Alibaba Cloud storage and domains designed to look connected to AOMEI. This changing delivery setup could make simple domain-blocking rules less reliable.

## How the malware chain worked

The first-stage program, CROSSROAD, arrived as upgrade-now.exe. It checked aspects of the computer and could download additional files, create a scheduled task and then delete its own copy.

The task launched a legitimate Radmin program every three hours. However, the Radmin process was placed alongside an attacker-created DLL named BlkScrDl.dll, which it loaded during startup.

That DLL helped start SHINYROAD, a backdoor that could communicate with the attackers’ systems. Later activity also involved ADAPTAGENT, a client for the Adaptix command-and-control framework, disguised as Nitro PDF software.

The use of real administration software and familiar product names can make a malicious process harder to distinguish from normal activity.

Other recent incidents, such as the DAEMON Tools malware supply-chain case, show how attackers can abuse trusted software channels to reach users.

On July 20, attackers added a second risk. They used an invisible, one-pixel notification window to make an AOMEI client request a remote file over WebDAV.

That request could prompt Windows to send NetNTLMv2 authentication data to an attacker-controlled server without a visible prompt. This technique is known as credential coercion: the victim’s computer is induced to attempt authentication to a remote location.

AOMEI’s server-side fix does not remove files already installed on affected computers. Organizations using AOMEI software should review endpoint and network records covering the campaign period, paying particular attention to unusual updater child processes, unexpected Radmin or Nitro-related scheduled tasks, and connections to the indicators below.

Analysts should also examine cached AOMEI configuration files and relevant proxy or firewall logs, since the live server may now return legitimate settings.

The incident also highlights a design issue for software vendors: HTTPS and a checksum supplied in an unsigned configuration file are not enough to prove an update is genuine.

Google recommends signed configuration files, cryptographic verification of downloaded files, and strict limits on which domains an updater may contact. Separating promotional pop-ups from update execution can also reduce the risk of one feature being misused to launch code.

The case echoes other short-lived supply-chain incidents, including a LiteLLM package compromise in which malicious releases were available for a limited period.

In both situations, a brief exposure window can still leave behind a longer incident-response task: find affected systems, assess what ran, and investigate whether credentials or other access were exposed.

articles.title: Google Unveils New Android AI Protections to Block Scam Calls, Phishing Links and OTP Theft
articles.summary: Google has announced a new set of Android security protections designed to stop mobile scams across calls, text messages, chat apps, web links, and account verification codes.
articles.content:
Google has announced a new set of Android security protections designed to stop mobile scams across calls, text messages, chat apps, web links, and account verification codes.

The update comes as criminals increasingly use spoofed phone numbers, fake bank alerts, phishing pages, remote screen sharing, and AI-generated voices to trick users into giving up money or login details.

Google said its existing AI-powered scam detection tools in Phone by Google and Google Messages already identify more than five million suspected scam calls and texts each month.

The new protections focus on preventing users from reaching the most dangerous stage of a scam. Instead of only blocking known malicious links or spam numbers.

Android will use a mix of on-device AI, cloud-based analysis, privacy protections, and real-time checks to identify suspicious behavior before victims share passwords, payment data, or one-time passcodes.

A key addition is an opt-in Enhanced Protection mode in Google Messages. Google said the setting will roll out in the coming weeks and will activate stronger protections for complex messaging scams.

This includes expanded Scam Detection using Google’s Private AI Compute platform, which allows Gemini models to review the context of a conversation with an unknown sender.

## Google Unveils New Android AI Protections

The aim is to spot slow-moving social engineering scams where criminals build trust over several messages before sending a fraudulent request or link. Google said the analysis occurs in an encrypted environment that Google employees cannot access.

Enhanced Protection will also strengthen link checks in Google Messages. Scammers frequently create new phishing domains that have not yet been added to threat blocklists, which can make standard URL filtering less effective.

Google said Gemini Nano, its on-device AI model, will combine real-time web signals with local analysis to assess unfamiliar links before a user opens them.

Android will also show redesigned warnings for links from numbers not saved in the user’s contacts. This provides an extra checkpoint before users visit a potential phishing page.

The company is also expanding scam alerts from Pixel devices to a wider Android ecosystem. Scam Detection in chat notifications can flag suspicious messages from supported chat apps directly in the notification panel, allowing users to see a warning before opening the message.

Google is working with Android device makers to bring the on-device feature to hundreds of millions of additional users later this year.

Google’s update also targets phone-based social engineering scams, particularly cases where criminals persuade victims to share their screen or redirect incoming calls.

Android will now automatically hide login fields and payment screens during active screen-sharing sessions in Chrome and Android WebView. The Protection is designed to stop fraudsters from viewing passwords, card details, and other sensitive information while guiding a victim through a fake support or banking process.

Another major safeguard addresses OTP theft through call forwarding. Threat actors may trick a user into entering a call-forwarding code, redirecting incoming calls containing verification codes to a criminal-controlled number.

Android will block apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warn users before a manually entered MMI forwarding code takes effect.

Security teams can also review related account takeover risks and prevention steps in Cyber Security News coverage of OTP bypass and MFA phishing campaigns and mobile banking malware.

Google is also expanding verified financial calls, a feature built with banks including Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco. The system checks whether the bank’s official app actually initiated a call claiming to come from a bank.

If verification fails, Android can end the call and alert the user. Google said the feature has blocked more than three million spoofed calls involving the two Brazilian banks since its June launch.

The announcement shows mobile security shifting from simple spam filtering to behavior-based fraud prevention. Users should still avoid sharing passwords, card information, recovery codes, or OTPs over calls and messages, even when the caller appears legitimate.

articles.title: Hackers Exploiting Plex Vulnerabilities in the Wild to Deploy Cryptominer Malware
articles.summary: Hackers are exploiting flaws in Plex Media Server to install cryptocurrency mining malware, with a researcher recording successful attacks against a honeypot on October 17, 2026.
articles.content:
Hackers are exploiting flaws in Plex Media Server to install cryptocurrency mining malware, with a researcher recording successful attacks against a honeypot on October 17, 2026.

The activity follows the release of Plex2Shell, a public exploit that chains four vulnerabilities to run code without logging in. Later observations also revealed proxy software running alongside the miner.

The findings from Boredhackerblog show active exploitation of an exposed test server, rather than scanning alone. However, the available evidence does not establish how many real servers have been compromised or identify the attackers behind the activity. The researcher also warned that restrictions on outbound traffic initially prevented collection of some payloads.

## How the Plex2Shell Exploit Works

Plex announced security updates on September 1, urging users to install Plex Media Server 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop 1.115.0. Its official security notice warned that NAS users might need to install updates manually. Cyber Security News previously covered the Plex security update and affected releases.

The exploit combines CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. According to the Plex2Shell repository, the chain starts with server-side request forgery, which tricks Plex into sending requests chosen by an attacker. It then reaches internal functions, gains access to owner-authorized requests, and writes a file to an attacker-selected location.

The final stage abuses the loading of an unsigned codec to execute code. The repository identifies versions before 1.43.3.10828 as vulnerable and lists 1.43.3.10861 as fixed. Although the exploit supports Linux and Windows targets, the reported honeypot activity involved a Linux-based Plex deployment running in Docker.

## Honeypot Captures Miner and Proxy Activity

In the researcher’s report, the first exploitation attempt came from 45.194.92[.]222. Further attempts involved 91.92.40[.]202 and 176.65.139[.]228. Recorded requests targeted /player/timeline/subscribe and included references to internal Plex services, an sslip.io hostname, and the Python-urllib/3.10 user agent.

After outbound access was enabled, the researcher observed downloads from 217.60.194[.]116 involving files named docker and x. Published artifacts included packed and unpacked samples, followed by an XMRig miner. Similar misuse of XMRig has appeared in other campaigns, including attacks against exposed Redis servers.

An update also reported a process named myawesomeproxy and traffic involving proxystream[.]st. The program displayed a message about external use of the device’s internet traffic. These observations raise concerns about proxy abuse, but they do not establish who operates this Plex campaign or prove a connection to a specific botnet.

Administrators should install the latest Plex release and verify the running version, particularly on NAS systems and Docker deployments. On Linux, review the Plex process tree for unexpected child processes, suspicious downloads, and unfamiliar mining or proxy programs. The researcher recommends examining processes with ps axjf.

Defenders can use the published packet captures to develop detections. Files marked “lab” come from controlled tests, not live attacks. The repository also warns that attackers can change ports, domains, and filenames, so matching only fixed indicators will leave detection gaps.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

The post Hackers Exploiting Plex Vulnerabilities in the Wild to Deploy Cryptominer Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

In an October 17 statement, the company linked the incident to a large-scale distillation attack and said it was working with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google to address it.

The affected group was limited to some Console users who had linked external providers. OpenCode said it had emailed everyone affected that morning and stated that users who did not receive an email were not impacted. The percentage refers to Console users, not the entire OpenCode user base.

## Legacy System Access Put Provider Keys at Risk

A notification shared in the supplied screenshot says OpenCode identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that it was already preparing to shut down. Third-party provider keys stored in users’ workspaces, including those for OpenAI and Anthropic, may have been exposed.

The notice asks recipients to revoke and replace those keys through each provider’s dashboard, update applications that use them, and review recent usage for unexpected activity. Its wording describes possible exposure rather than confirming that every affected key was stolen or used.

OpenCode’s public statement does not explain how attackers gained access, how long they remained inside, or how many keys were involved. It also does not name an attacker or provide technical evidence showing how the breach supported the reported distillation activity.

Distillation involves training one AI model using responses generated by another. In an unauthorized campaign, attackers can collect large amounts of model output without permission. Cybersecurity News previously covered Anthropic’s warnings about large scale distillation attacks, explaining how repeated requests can help transfer capabilities between models.

However, OpenCode has not explained whether exposed credentials were used to make those requests. Its statement establishes a reported connection, not a complete account of the attack. There is also no confirmed loss figure in the public disclosure.

The wider risk of exposed credentials has appeared in earlier reporting on API keys found in public web data. That separate case illustrates why secret storage and removal matter, but it does not establish a shared attacker or method here.

## Affected Users Urged to Replace Keys

For notified users, the immediate response is the key replacement process described in the warning. Reviewing provider usage alongside recent billing records can help identify requests that need investigation. Replacing a key also requires updating every application that depends on it.

OpenCode said the incident remained ongoing when it published its statement and that it could not share more details. A fuller technical report would help establish the entry point, the scope of credential exposure, and whether unauthorized model requests occurred.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

The post OpenCode Security Breach Exposes Third-Party API Keys of its Console Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Claude AI Solves 25-Year NSA Cryptography Mystery in Just 30 Minutes
articles.summary: Anthropic says an internal Claude research model has traced the origins of five NSA-supplied elliptic curve seeds in under 30 minutes, answering a cryptography question that remained open for roughly 25 years. The finding explains how important publi
articles.content:
Anthropic says an internal Claude research model has traced the origins of five NSA-supplied elliptic curve seeds in under 30 minutes, answering a cryptography question that remained open for roughly 25 years. The finding explains how important public security parameters were chosen, rather than exposing secret keys or breaking encryption.

In a report published October 16, 2026, researchers said the seeds behind NIST curves P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 came from lrand48, an older C library random-number generator initialized with Unix timestamps. The result challenges a long-running theory that the values were hashes of humorous phrases.

## NSA Curve Seeds Raised Questions

NIST adopted ECDSA, the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, in its FIPS 186-2 standard in 2000. Digital signatures help verify who signed data and whether it has changed. The standard published seeds used by a SHA-1-based process to derive curve parameters, but did not explain where those seeds originated.

That missing history left room for claims that the NSA might have selected curves with hidden weaknesses. Researchers had no demonstrated attack against these curves, but lacked a clear account of their selection. Former NSA mathematician Jerry Solinas recalled phrases such as “Give Bob and Jerry a raise,” sending earlier searches toward possible hash inputs.

The stakes extend beyond academic debate. Cybersecurity News previously covered Apple’s PQ3 iMessage protocol, which uses ECDSA with P-256 for message authentication. Understanding the history of these shared parameters helps explain why trust in curve selection matters across widely used services.

## Claude Rebuilt the Generation Process

Instead of following the phrase theory, Claude examined generators common in 1990s software. It built a scanner covering 34 combinations of generators and output slices, looking for patterns inside the published seeds.

Some binary-curve seeds showed a clear clue. Their 32-bit words consistently had a zero in the highest bit, matching lrand48, which returns 31 bits from a 48-bit internal state. Claude recovered candidate states by testing the 17 hidden bits and checking subsequent outputs.

The prime-curve seeds required another step because they retained only eight bits from each generator output. Claude used the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász lattice reduction algorithm, or LLL, to recover internal states from these partial values. Five NIST seeds and five ANSI X9.62 example seeds matched the same construction.

Running the generator backward revealed initialization values corresponding to dates between May 1997 and April 1998. For P-256, the published seed was the 1,842nd candidate from a run initialized on August 16, 1997, at 01:52:34 UTC. Each candidate contained 20 bytes.

Four binary-curve seeds also matched the generator. Their values suggest a clock value divided by two, although the researchers describe that interpretation as a possibility, not a confirmed fact.

Anthropic stressed that this is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or newly discovered ECDSA weakness. These are public curve-generation seeds, not private signing keys. Reconstructing them does not let an attacker forge signatures. The researchers say the simple, repeatable process makes deliberate manipulation less plausible.

The work adds another example of AI-assisted cryptography research, following Cybersecurity News coverage of Claude’s analysis of cryptographic weaknesses. Here, however, the outcome is historical clarity rather than an improved attack.

Claude also traced base-point generation for P-192 and five ANSI example curves to FreeLIP, a long-integer arithmetic package. Base points are fixed starting points used to calculate public keys, and their origins are separate from the curve seeds.

The account is not complete. B-163’s seed remains unexplained, as do several base points. Researchers also found skipped candidates that appeared suitable, including P-256 candidate 876, without knowing why they were rejected. The findings therefore strengthen confidence without proving every selection decision was harmless.

Anthropic published reproduction code so others can check the matches. The Internet Security Research Group will receive the $36,864 bounty. The report calls for no changes to deployed systems because of this discovery alone.

An EDR alert reveals an attack. But can it tell the full story? Discover how to reconstruct the attack timeline.

The post Claude AI Solves 25-Year NSA Cryptography Mystery in Just 30 Minutes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Google Fixes 10 Chrome Vulnerabilities, Including Memory Corruption Flaw Found With Claude AI
articles.summary: Google released a Chrome Stable security update fixing 10 vulnerabilities across Windows, Mac, and Linux, including a high-severity DOM memory corruption flaw reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic with Claude AI.
articles.content:
Google released a Chrome Stable security update fixing 10 vulnerabilities across Windows, Mac, and Linux, including a high-severity DOM memory corruption flaw reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic with Claude AI.

The update also addresses one critical, six high-severity, and three medium-severity vulnerabilities. Google announced the update on October 15, 2026.

Google is rolling out Chrome versions 155.0.8059.84/.85 for Windows and Mac, and version 155.0.8059.84 for Linux over the coming days and weeks. Users should install the update when it becomes available and check Chrome’s About page to prompt an update check.

The most serious issue is CVE-2026-110922, a critical use-after-free flaw in Chrome’s Prerender feature. Google credits Xinyang Ge with reporting it on October 2.

A use-after-free bug occurs when software tries to use memory after it has been released. Depending on how an attacker can reach the flaw, this type of error may cause a crash or allow memory corruption. Google has not published further technical details and has not said the issue is being exploited.

CVE-2026-110913 is a high-severity memory corruption flaw in Chrome’s DOM, the browser system that represents and manages the structure of web pages.

## Google Fixes 10 Chrome Vulnerabilities

Ge reported the bug on September 29, with Claude’s assistance. Google’s release note does not explain how the issue was found, whether Claude identified the flaw or helped with analysis, or what steps were involved. It does, however, publicly credit the AI’s assistance in the report.

The other high-severity fixes affect V8, Chrome’s JavaScript engine, as well as Core and SVG. They include two additional use-after-free flaws in V8, CVE-2026-110919 and CVE-2026-110921, and memory corruption issues CVE-2026-110918, CVE-2026-110917, and CVE-2026-110920. The reports came from Ge, Google, and researcher C0rk1.

The three medium-severity bugs involve improper input validation in Desktop, a use-after-free issue in Compositing, and memory corruption in Workers.

Google credited its own researchers with reporting these flaws. Together, the list shows that this release addresses problems in separate browser components rather than a single feature or subsystem.

Google says detailed bug information may remain restricted until most users have installed the fixes. This can limit what researchers and users can learn about the vulnerabilities while the update is spreading.

The company also said it uses tools such as AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, libFuzzer, and AFL to find security bugs during development.

Chrome updates are delivered gradually, so users may not receive the new version at the same time. Check the browser’s About Google Chrome page and restart it if prompted to complete installation. Organizations should follow their normal browser update process and confirm that managed devices receive the fixed release.

This update follows other recent Chrome security coverage, including Google’s earlier report on a large Chrome vulnerability update and coverage of multiple Chrome flaws. Google’s Stable Channel announcement and Chrome Security page provide the primary release information.

Google released a Chrome Stable security update fixing 10 vulnerabilities across Windows, Mac, and Linux, including a high-severity DOM memory corruption flaw reported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic with Claude AI.

The update also addresses one critical, six high-severity, and three medium-severity vulnerabilities. Google announced the update on October 15, 2026.

Google is rolling out Chrome versions 155.0.8059.84/.85 for Windows and Mac, and version 155.0.8059.84 for Linux over the coming days and weeks. Users should install the update when it becomes available and check Chrome’s About page to prompt an update check.

The most serious issue is CVE-2026-110922, a critical use-after-free flaw in Chrome’s Prerender feature. Google credits Xinyang Ge with reporting it on October 2.

A use-after-free bug occurs when software tries to use memory after it has been released. Depending on how an attacker can reach the flaw, this type of error may cause a crash or allow memory corruption. Google has not published further technical details and has not said the issue is being exploited.

CVE-2026-110913 is a high-severity memory corruption flaw in Chrome’s DOM, the browser system that represents and manages the structure of web pages.

Ge reported the bug on September 29, with Claude’s assistance. Google’s release note does not explain how the issue was found, whether Claude identified the flaw or helped with analysis, or what steps were involved. It does, however, publicly credit the AI’s assistance in the report.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Collabora Online Flaw to Backdoor Nextcloud Servers
articles.summary: Hackers are exploiting a critical flaw in the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud, with users reporting web shells on compromised servers.
articles.content:
Hackers are exploiting a critical flaw in the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud, with users reporting web shells on compromised servers.

Tracked as CVE-2026-110447, the vulnerability allows remote attackers to run operating system commands without logging in. It affects the richdocumentscode app before version 26.4.303 and carries a CVSS v4 score of 9.2.

The GitHub Advisory Database entry states that attackers exploited the flaw during September and October 2026. An October 3 warning on the Nextcloud community forum reported that users had found web shells on their servers.

These malicious scripts can let attackers run commands and maintain access after the initial break-in. Available reports do not identify a specific threat group or state how many servers were breached.

The flaw sits in proxy.php, part of the app that runs Collabora’s built-in document server inside a Nextcloud deployment. According to Collabora’s security advisory, a crafted request can cause the server to execute an operating system command as the web server user. The issue is classified as CWE-78, or operating system command injection.

Attackers do not need an account, and no user interaction is required. However, exploitation depends on one important condition. The built-in CODE server must not be running when the malicious request reaches the vulnerable code. This can happen during a container restart, an upgrade, or after a crash, creating an attack window during otherwise routine maintenance.

## Hackers Exploit Collabora Online Flaw

Commands run with the permissions of the web server account, not automatically as root. Even so, the Github advisory rates the potential impact on data privacy, file integrity, and service availability as high. The reported web shells show why affected administrators should treat this as more than a software update task.

The issue affects the Collabora Online Built-in CODE Server app, rather than every Nextcloud or Collabora installation. Standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected.

Collabora also confirms that this is a different attack path from CVE-2025-66208, and installing the earlier vulnerability’s fix does not block this exploit.

Unlike the credential theft discussed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of infostealer-driven cloud breaches, this attack needs no stolen password.

It is also separate from previously reported Nextcloud desktop client code execution flaws, which involved unsafe URL handling rather than this server-side proxy.

Administrators should upgrade richdocumentscode to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove it. Turning off the app alone does not prevent exploitation. According to Collabora, users running end-of-life Nextcloud versions 29 or earlier should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the affected app.

For previously exposed systems, the community warning also recommends checking for unexpected PHP files. Updating closes the vulnerable entry point, but should not be treated as proof that an existing web shell has been removed. Reported compromises make checking for signs of intrusion an important follow-up to patching.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.summary: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that ar
articles.content:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

articles.title: ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests
articles.summary: A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that t
articles.content:
A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle “Rey,” was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey’s father — Royal Jordanian Airlines.

The logo for Jeppesen ForeFlight, a business unit divested last year by the aerospace firm Boeing.

On October 3, Reuters cited three unnamed sources saying a suspected ShinyHunters member in Amman named Saif Al-din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. KrebsOnSecurity identified Rey as Khader in a November 2025 profile, in which the young man admitted working with multiple ransomware groups.

Rey was featured again in a September 28 exclusive about the Dutch police arresting 24-year-old convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap on suspicion of aiding in data thefts and extortions by ShinyHunters. The story noted that immediately following the Dutchman’s arrest on the evening of September 15, Rey assumed control over the ShinyHunters brand and boasted publicly about stealing highly sensitive data from the FBI and extorting the ransomware group Cl0p.

Rey taunted both the FBI and Cl0p with memes posted to his longtime account on Twitter/X, while simultaneously including images of the avatar used by Van Der Stap’s former hacker alias “Umbreon” in an apparent attempt to frame the Dutchman for both hacks.

A taunting meme uploaded to Twitter/X by Rey on Sept. 22. A giant sized version of the Pokemon character Umbreon can be seen in the bottom left.

As noted in our September 28 report, ShinyHunters gained access to the FBI site and other victims by exploiting a vulnerability (CVE-2026-35273) in PeopleSoft, a software-as-a-service platform from the tech giant Oracle that is broadly used by companies to manage hiring and human resources, benefits and payroll. Oracle quickly issued a fix for CVE-2026-35273, which ShinyHunters first began exploiting as a zero-day in June, and at the time Mandiant released web application firewall rules intended for organizations that couldn’t apply the security update quickly enough.

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer in June that the original goal behind exploiting the PeopleSoft vulnerability was to breach the FBI’s own PeopleSoft database, but the hackers said those attacks were unsuccessful for some reason. In recent weeks, however, ShinyHunters turned to a well-known URL-encoding trick to bypass Mandiant’s suggested web application firewall rules.

In a report released Sept. 25, security experts at Mandiant and the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) confirmed that ShinyHunters had mass-exploited the PeopleSoft vulnerability to steal data from dozens of systems across a range of industries, including higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.

Reuters reported October 5 that the FBI has removed a contractor at Accenture over their failure to patch the FBI recruitment website hacked by ShinyHunters, which exposed sensitive data on more than 5,000 FBI personnel, including each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

## ‘REY’ MEANS KING, AS IN ROYAL

According to two sources familiar with the ShinyHunters investigation, a navigation and digital aviation unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing was among the victims that ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting when Rey was apprehended by Jordanian authorities.

Those sources said the FBI’s investigation into ShinyHunters gained renewed urgency with the group’s attempted extortion of the former Boeing unit, which allegedly included the theft of sensitive information that sources said could pose operational safety and security risks.

In a brief statement shared with KrebsOnSecurity, Boeing acknowledged the extortion attempts by ShinyHunters, and said the incident concerned data stolen from Jeppesen ForeFlight, a subsidiary that Boeing sold in November 2025 to the private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $10.55 billion.

One of the coordinators of that harassment campaign repeatedly portrayed Rey as clueless greenhorn who sought to ride the coattails of a cybercriminal brand that has long enjoyed a reputation for ruthlessly selling or publishing data stolen from victim companies who refuse to give in to extortion demands.

A flash notice on ShinyHunters released by the FBI on May 15, 2026.

The public notice warned the group has been known to pursue a number of different victim harassment strategies, from sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members to in some cases swatting victims.
